# A dismissed rail reveal animates an empty slot: the pane is detached on the transition frame

## Context

Reported by the operator on the Workstation, 2026-09-02 ~19:00Z, after pulling `dev` and rebuilding themes: a dismissed rail reveal still disappears at once. Their second reading is the one that located it — *"ESC key also hides instantly => the transition starts, and a couple of frames later (way too early) => removeDom"*.

So the exit motion from #18116 / PR #18118 is **not** broken: the `-leaving` class lands and the keyframes run. Something else empties the panel while they run.

## The Problem

**The two-phase hide defers the overlay's `hidden` class. It never deferred the content's removal.**

Measured on `dev@ec6856b804` with a throwaway probe on the `dock-rail-origin` fixture — reveal, let the entry settle, press Escape, read while `-leaving` is on the node:

```
before dismiss  slot children : 1
during leave    slot children : 0        ← the pane is already gone
during leave    slot animation: ["neo-dock-reveal-to-left"]
during leave    root animation: ["neo-dock-reveal-fade-out"]
```

**An empty slot slides out.** The root fades, the slot travels back to its edge, and there is nothing inside either of them — which is indistinguishable from an instant hide to anyone watching, and exactly what the operator saw.

**Why the merged witness passes.** `DockRailRevealExit.spec.mjs` asserts the overlay is `-leaving` and not `-hidden`, that `display` is not `none`, that `pointer-events` is `none`, and that the root and **slot** carry the expected animation names. Every one of those is true of an empty slot. The spec reads the slot's *animation*; it never reads the slot's *contents*. Reviewed and approved by me on PR #18118 — the gap is in the assertion set, not in the implementation it witnesses.

## The Architectural Reality

- `Neo.dashboard.dock.interaction.Rail#onRevealStateChange` (`:648`) runs on every machine transition and calls `syncRevealOverlay()`.
- `syncRevealOverlay` (`:802`) resolves `railItem` from `machine.revealedItemId` — **`null` once dismissed** — pushes the snapshot onto the overlay, and then calls `me.syncRevealPane(railItem)` with that `null`.
- `syncRevealPane` (`:925`): `nextId = railItem?.dockItemId ?? null`; `currentId !== nextId`, so it reaches `slot.remove(child, …)` and adds nothing back. **Synchronous, on the transition frame.**
- `Neo.dashboard.dock.interaction.RevealOverlay#syncRevealMotion` meanwhile takes the `visible → hidden` boundary into `beginRevealLeave()`, which keeps the overlay mounted until the root's `animationend` (`completeRevealLeave`) or the `MotionSignal.FAIL_SAFE_MS` backstop.

The two mechanisms are unaware of each other: the overlay owns "when does the DOM go", the rail owns "when does the pane go", and only the first learned about the exit.

## The Fix

The pane detach has to wait for the same seam the hidden class already waits for.

1. **Defer the detach to the end of the leave.** The overlay already has the terminal — `completeRevealLeave()` — and already knows it is leaving (`revealLeaving`). The rail's `syncRevealPane(null)` should not run while a leave is in flight; it should run when the leave settles (or when the overlay hides without one, the unmounted path).
2. **Keep the shape one-way.** A re-entry during a leave cancels it (`cancelRevealLeave`) and may retarget to a *different* item — so a deferred detach must not fire after the overlay has re-entered, and must not detach the newly revealed pane. The generation/`revealShownItemId` bookkeeping added for the retarget (#18117) is the existing precedent for distinguishing those cases.
3. **The engine seam, not a rail timer.** No `setTimeout` matching the token duration: that reintroduces the two-clocks problem #18117 explicitly avoided. The signal is the overlay's own end event.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC-1** While the overlay carries `-leaving`, the pane slot still contains its pane. Red-first on `dev`: the probe above returns `0` children today, `1` after. Component witness on the rail fixture.
- [ ] **AC-2** The pane is detached once the leave completes — the slot is empty (or reparented back to its cache) only after `-hidden` lands, and the pane instance is not destroyed by the deferral.
- [ ] **AC-3** A re-entry during a leave keeps its pane: dismiss, re-open the **same** item mid-exit, and the slot holds that pane throughout with no detach afterwards.
- [ ] **AC-4** A retarget during a leave detaches the outgoing pane and mounts the incoming one exactly once: dismiss, click a **different** rail item mid-exit, and the slot ends holding the new pane.
- [ ] **AC-5** The existing exit arm is tightened so it cannot pass on an empty slot again — it asserts slot **contents** alongside the animation names it already reads.
- [ ] **AC-6** `DockRailRevealExit`, `DockRailRevealRetarget`, `DockRailRevealOrigin`, `DockRailRevealIframe`, `unit/dashboard` and `component/dashboard` stay green.
- [ ] **AC-7 (e2e, operator-reported path)** An e2e arm on the Workstation's own rails proves a running exit animation **and** a mounted pane for its duration, for both dismissal routes the operator hit: Escape and focus-leave. This is the arm the component fixture could not supply — the report came from the served app, and the component witness was green throughout.

## Out of Scope

- The exit motion itself (#18116 / PR #18118) — the keyframes and the two-phase class flip are correct and stay.
- The retarget slide (#18117 / PR #18120) — its swap generations are unaffected; AC-4 only pins that a retarget still detaches once.
- T2's true sliding cross-fade (an outgoing layer that keeps the previous pane mounted *after* the incoming one arrives) — a different feature, still a design leaf.

## Avoided Traps

- **Asserting the animation instead of the thing being animated.** This is the defect that produced the report: the witness read the slot's `animationName` and its `display`, all of which an empty slot satisfies. Any new arm must read what is *inside* the animating element, not only that it animates.
- **A timer in the rail.** Matching the exit duration with a `setTimeout` would put the paint and the detach on two clocks — the exact drift #18117 removed for the keyframes. The overlay's end event is the one signal.
- **Deferring unconditionally.** A dismissal with no DOM (the unmounted path) settles synchronously and must still detach; a deferral that waits for an end event that never comes would leak the pane into a hidden overlay.
- **Reading the fixture as the app.** The component fixture and the Workstation disagreed here — the fixture was green while the served app was visibly wrong — which is why AC-7 exists rather than another component arm alone.

## Related

- #18116 / PR #18118 — the exit motion this completes; its witness is the one AC-5 tightens.
- #18117 / PR #18120 — the retarget slide, whose generation bookkeeping is the precedent for AC-3/AC-4.
- #18074 / PR #18079 — the entry motion.

## Operator corroboration: the theme asymmetry is predicted by the defect, and it sharpens the ACs

@tobiu, following the report: *"inside the light theme, there is a slide-out. very fast. i can not really see it inside the dark theme."*

That is consistent with the root cause above and worth recording, because it explains why the bug reads as *two different bugs* depending on the skin — and why an eye-read in one theme would have been reassuring for the wrong reason.

**What is actually sliding is the empty chrome.** The pane is detached on the transition frame, so what travels is the overlay root and its (now empty) header and slot. The root's exit is `neo-dock-reveal-fade-out` → `opacity: 0`, so the only thing visible for those milliseconds is the overlay's own surface fading.

**And that surface is deliberately the host's.** From the reveal chrome floor (#18080 / PR #18085):

```scss
--dock-reveal-background: var(--neo-background-color, #fff);
--dock-reveal-border    : 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 22%, transparent);
--dock-reveal-shadow    : 0 0 0 1px color-mix(in srgb, currentColor 8%, transparent),
                          0 12px 32px rgb(0 0 0 / 28%);
```

The overlay and the pane beneath it are **the same colour by design** — the only separation is the 22%-alpha hairline and the elevation shadow, and both fade out with the root. On a dark ground that is a nearly-invisible box dissolving; on a light ground the hairline and the shadow carry just enough contrast to register as movement. Same defect, two readings.

**"Very fast" is the token, not a second bug:** `--dock-transition-duration-reveal` is `var(--motion-panel, 280ms)` — the same value the entry uses, and the value #18074 landed against the operator's "e.g. 300ms". It is not obviously wrong; it *reads* wrong when there is no content travelling, because 280 ms of empty chrome is a flicker while 280 ms of a panel sliding under its strip is a motion. Whether it still reads too fast once the pane is restored is a judgement to make **after** the fix, on the fixed thing — not a knob to turn now.

### Two AC additions

- [ ] **AC-8** The witness runs in **both** neo themes. A dark-theme-only eye-read would have shown almost nothing here; a light-theme-only one would have shown "a fast slide" and been called working. Neither is sufficient alone, and the existing exit arm has no theme dimension.
- [ ] **AC-9** After the fix, the exit is re-read by eye in both themes before the duration is discussed. If it still reads too fast with the pane mounted, that is a token conversation (`--motion-panel`) on its own ticket, not a change smuggled into this one.

### The instrument note worth keeping

This is the second time today the same class has bitten on this surface: a green witness that reads a **property of the animation** rather than **what is being animated**. The spec asserts the slot's `animationName`; the operator's eye asserts whether anything moved. The eye was right, and it was right in only one of the two themes — so the theme dimension is not decoration on AC-8, it is the difference between seeing the bug and being reassured by it.

🖖 Grace
